description:
Prime Innovators
MCA students from The Neotia University, India, building the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a free browser-based space academy with quizzes, mini-games (oxygen, docking, Mars landing) and badges using real NASA data. Skills: [your skills]. We’re looking for a UI/UX designer, a game developer (Canvas/Phaser) and a content researcher. Beginners welcome. Join us to build a fun, portfolio-worthy project!
summary: SOL BASE: Mission Trainer is a free, browser-based game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost and learn that in space, nothing is free. Players choose a site (Moon: 14-day night, ~1.3s radio delay; Mars: dust storms, 3-22 minute delay), a difficulty (Cadet, Astro, Cmdr), a mission, and a session length, with time compressed so a full mission fits in 30 minutes. They manage just three resources, Power, Life Support, and Food, plus a radiation Shield. Before every action, a Cost Card shows what it gains, what it costs, and what it risks, so no choice is free. Time-lapse speeds up the days but always stops at a crisis, such as a solar flare or dust storm, where players respond with a short puzzle. Crises are driven by real NASA DONKI space-weather data, chosen as live or archived and labeled with its source and date. Communication delay means Mission Control’s advice arrives late on Mars. After each run, a debrief shows the real NASA event and what real mission planners would do. Plain-language tooltips, colorblind-safe design, and no account needed make it easy for classrooms. Different real events make every playthrough new, so kids learn from failure and understand how real missions are planned.
details:
SOL BASE is an interactive 3D space habitat engineering simulator where students, educators, and space enthusiasts design and operate lunar and Martian outposts under real aerospace constraints. Players select a landing site (Lunar South Pole or Mars — Jezero Crater), difficulty level (Cadet, Astronaut, or Commander), mission scenario, and space-weather mode (Archived 2024 Solar Cycle 25 or Live NASA DONKI). Inside a Three.js 3D terrain, players place power, life-support, greenhouse, research, and radiation-shielding modules, inspect Gain / Pay / Risk Cost Cards before every build or rover expedition, balance live Oxygen/Water and Power budgets, and protect a four-astronaut crew through 14-day lunar nights, Martian dust storms, and solar proton events. Under the hood, an Express backend proxies and normalizes all 11 official NASA DONKI endpoints (FLR, CME, CMEAnalysis, GST, IPS, SEP, MPC, RBE, HSS, WSAEnlilSimulations, and notifications), feeding real solar flare classes, CME speeds, and proton flux telemetry into the simulation. When resources turn critical or storms strike, color-coded green/yellow/red telemetry pulses activate, time auto-pauses, and the onboard ARIA assistant delivers spoken and visual alerts while players solve diagnostic engineering puzzles, shelter crew, sinter regolith shielding, and navigate realistic Earth–Mars light-speed communication delays.

By turning abstract closed-loop life-support math, thermodynamics, and radiation physics into visual cause-and-effect gameplay, SOL BASE delivers strong educational benefits for both solo learners and classrooms. Students can research three tiers of real NASA/ESA technologies (including aeroponic hydroponics, perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells, Bosch CO₂ reduction, and compact fusion) and collaborate in real-time 6-character Co-op Classroom Rooms with assigned crew roles, live trade-off voting, and teacher controls to pause, resume, or trigger solar flare drills. Every mission ends with an automatic Mission Debrief containing a timestamped decision ledger, NASA dataset citations, mission badges, and .txt, .pdf, and print-ready take-home reports. Its intended impact is to build systems-level STEM literacy and show learners that off-world survival has no free upgrades—every engineering choice trades off energy, water, metal, regolith, and crew safety.

We built the application using TypeScript, TSX, HTML5, CSS3, and JSON, powered by React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4, Three.js, Lucide React, and Motion on the frontend, and Node.js, Express 4, and Socket.IO on the backend. Browser-native Web Audio API and Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) drive procedural ambient sound and ARIA voice warnings, while automated quality checks run through Node's node:test runner (tsx), TypeScript (tsc --noEmit), and Playwright headless Chromium on standard workstation hardware and cloud containers.

The project stands out creatively through its "No Free Choices" Cost Cards, live/archived NASA solar storm telemetry directly driving radiation shelter timing, Mars light-delay crisis communications, ISS Veggie-modeled hydroponic care controls, and an automated engineering ledger linking player decisions to NASA datasets. Throughout development, our team carefully accounted for NASA DEMO_KEY rate limits and school network restrictions (solved with a 15-minute server cache and automatic historical archive fallback), low-end school hardware performance (via adaptive software-WebGL detection in Three.js), accessibility (pairing pulse colors with shape/icon indicators, tabular numbers, audio mute toggles, and a 60-second interactive tutorial), and time-compression tuning so multi-week planetary missions remain scientifically grounded within a 15-to-30-minute class session.
